naming: PAGASA expects a strong to very strong El Niño. “Super El Niño” is the media’s name for it.

prepare.d: PAGASA’s outlook has Benguet in a dry spell by the end of November and in drought from December.

items.t: Store water while the rains last
items.d: Clean and cover tanks and drums now. Baguio’s planners warn of possible drought from December into summer 2027.

items.t: Fix leaks and follow the city’s advisories
items.d: Baguio’s water monitoring reached the orange phase on Oct 15, which means stronger conservation. The city now issues daily advisories.

items.t: Farmers: plan crops now
items.d: DA-Cordillera urges early action on irrigation, crop planning and insurance. Ask your Municipal Agriculture Office about drought-tolerant seed.

dry1.d: Two months in a row of below-normal rain.

items.t: Use less water every day
items.d: Use a tabo instead of a hose. Not every toilet use needs a flush. Reuse rinse water on plants.

items.t: Keep stored water covered
items.d: DOH says covering containers keeps stored water from being contaminated. Open water also breeds mosquitoes.

items.t: Don’t burn trash or brush
items.d: Grass dries fast. Benguet had 38 forest fires from January to early April 2026, against 14 in all of 2025.

items.t: Plan around rationing
items.d: December’s tourist peak lands in the expected drought. Fill containers when supply runs, and set drinking water aside.

items.t: Drink only safe water
items.d: Boil water if you’re unsure of the source. Diarrhea, vomiting or weakness needs a health worker; untreated, it can turn fatal.

items.t: Farmers: watch for frost
items.d: Frost hits highland farms in Atok, Buguias, Kibungan and Mankayan in the cold months, roughly December to February. Sprinklers run before sunrise wash ice off leaves.

drought.d: Rain way below normal for months.

items.t: See smoke? Call 911 early
items.d: Forest fires peak in these months. In April 2026, Itogon suspended trekking at six mountain sites because of fires.

items.t: Use every litre twice
items.d: Rinse water can flush toilets and water plants. Skip the garden hose and the bidet.

items.t: Mind the heat in the lower towns
items.d: Drink 8 to 10 glasses a day. Move anyone with heat stroke somewhere cool, give water, then take them to a clinic.

after.d: PAGASA’s outlook ends in March. It says El Niño could last through the first half of 2027.

items.t: Keep saving until PAGASA calls the end
items.d: Dry conditions can outlast the outlook. Follow PAGASA’s monthly El Niño advisories.

items.t: Clean containers before the rains
items.d: Empty, scrub and cover stored-water containers so they stay clean when the rains come back.

items.t: Farmers: ask about recovery support
items.d: DA-Cordillera runs seed, fertilizer and irrigation programs. Start with your Municipal Agriculture Office.

items.t: Store water in clean, covered containers.
Follow Baguio’s daily water advisories. The city has been in the orange phase since Oct 15.
Use a tabo instead of a hose, and skip the bidet.
Not every toilet use needs a flush.
Fix dripping taps and running toilets.
Reuse rinse and laundry water to flush and water plants.
Visitors count too. Baguio’s daytime population nearly doubles, and December’s peak lands in the expected drought.
Drink 8 to 10 glasses of water a day.
Drink only water from clean sources. Boil it if you’re unsure.
Diarrhea, vomiting or weakness: see a health worker. Untreated cases can need hospital care.
Fever with chills, headache or joint pain: get checked at the nearest health facility.
Heat stroke: move the person somewhere cool, let them rest and drink water, then take them to a clinic.
Older people, small children and people with illnesses are most at risk.
Outdoors, wear a hat or carry an umbrella, dress light and use sunscreen.
Don’t burn trash, grass or brush, and no kaingin.
Put cigarettes out fully and dispose of the butts properly.
No bonfires or campfires in forests and grasslands.
Keep matches and lighters away from children.
Never leave an outdoor fire unattended.
Unplug appliances you aren’t using, and avoid octopus connections.
See smoke? Call 911 right away.
Ask your Municipal Agriculture Office about drought-tolerant seed and crop insurance.
Mulch to hold moisture in the soil and keep weeds down.
Harvest rainwater. Small irrigation and water-impounding near farms helps.
Time planting so young crops miss the December to February frost.
On frost nights, sprinklers run before sunrise wash ice off leaves. Plastic tunnels also help.
Rice: alternate wetting and drying cuts water use by about 30% with no yield penalty.
DA-CAR lists mungbean, cowpea, cassava and sweet potato as El Niño alternative crops.
